meta.source: Computed by npm run build:data from data/decision-rules.json, data/lifespans.json, data/cost-ranges.json, data/uef-ranges.json, data/hot-water-use.json and data/energy-prices.json with assets/js/formulas.js
meta.notes: Default result, repair limits by type, energy comparison and cross-check for the repair-or-replace tool. Replacement prices are installed prices (equipment + labor + permit and haul-away, U.S. average) from the shared cost model in assets/js/cost-model.js.

defaultInputs.note: Example inputs for the server-rendered default result; not data about any real home.

default.headline: Repair it: the quote is small and the heater is within its normal life
default.explain: At 8.0 years it is within its normal life: 62% of a 13-year typical life used. The repair is 14% of the replacement price.
default.formula:
Expected life (gas tank) = 13 years; "old" from 0.75 × 13 = 9.8 years
Life used = 8.0 ÷ 13 = 62%
Repair share = $250 ÷ $1,809 = 14%
Rules: leak or flood → replace; age ≥ 15 years (top of the life range) → replace soon; share > 50% → replace; old and share > 25% → replace; old → borderline; share > 25% → borderline; else repair. Rusty hot water, or rumbling once old, moves the answer one step toward replace
Running cost (55 gal/day, 67 °F rise): Gas tank UEF 0.635 = $262/yr; Gas tank (high efficiency, ENERGY STAR) UEF 0.9 = $185/yr; difference $77/yr
default.sources: Rules: ours, stated on /methodology. Typical life: DOE (13 years for tanks, 20 for tankless). New-unit price: typical installed price, U.S. average (equipment from Home Depot listings, 2026-11-12, plus labor, permit and haul-away from our cost model); type your own quote if you have one. See our rules checked against Rheem and A. O. Smith guidance.

rules.note: Since audit fix F-08 (2026-11-14): a unit at or past the high end of its life range (data/lifespans.json) is "replace soon" whatever the repair costs; rusty hot water (always) or rumbling once the unit is old (ageShare of its typical life) moves the verdict one step toward replace, because Rheem lists both among the signs a heater should be replaced.

defaultInputs.note: Example inputs for the server-rendered default result; not data about any real home.

symptoms.label: Water leaking from the tank itself
symptoms.note: A leak from the tank body cannot be fixed; the heater has to be replaced. Check first that the water is not coming from a pipe, valve or fitting above it, because leaks are often in the plumbing, not the heater.

symptoms.label: Drip at a valve, pipe or fitting
symptoms.note: Small valve or fitting leaks are often repairable.

symptoms.label: Rusty or discolored hot water
symptoms.note: Rheem lists rusty or discolored hot water as a sign the heater should be replaced. Rusty water can also come from old pipes, so check whether the cold water is clear.

symptoms.label: Rumbling or popping noise
symptoms.note: Persistent rumbling or popping comes from hardened sediment on the tank floor; Rheem counts it among the signs of replacement.

symptoms.label: No hot water, or not enough
symptoms.note: Often a heating element, thermostat or (on gas units) the ignition parts. Heating elements, thermostats and anode rods are designed to be replaced.

symptoms.label: Relief valve dripping or discharging
symptoms.note: The temperature and pressure (T&P) relief valve is a safety device. Never cap or plug it or its discharge pipe; have the cause checked.

symptoms.label: Heater was in a flood
symptoms.note: If the heater was flooded or its controls were under water, the manufacturer says the whole unit must be replaced.

kwh.label: Electricity price
kwh.note: Use 0 only if your water heating is fully covered by your own solar panels.
